records.source: ἀτενίσας δὲ ὁ Παῦλος τῷ συνεδρίῳ εἶπεν· Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί, ἐγὼ πάσῃ συνειδήσει ἀγαθῇ πεπολίτευμαι τῷ θεῷ ἄχρι ταύτης τῆς ἡμέρας.
records.gloss: Having looked intently then Paul at the council said, Men, brothers, I in all conscience good have lived as a citizen to God until this the day.
pieces: Paul fixed his eyes on the council and said, "Brothers, I have conducted my life before God with a fully clear conscience up to this very day."

L.1: And Paul, having looked intently at the council, said, "Men, brothers, I have lived as a citizen before God in all good conscience until this day."

R.1: Paul looked hard at the members of the council. He said, "My brothers, all my life I have done what I knew God wanted me to do. My conscience is clear before God, even today."

decisions.choice: the council: the Sanhedrin, the high council of the Jews in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The tribune had ordered the chief priests and the whole council to meet so that he could learn what Paul was accused of (22:30). The council was made up of chief priests, elders and scribes (4:5, 4:15), with the high priest presiding.

decisions.choice: Men, brothers: a formal address to the members of the council, who were all men
alternatives: an address to a mixed audience
decisions.reason: The members of the council were men, so the address is not widened to include women here, as it is not in 7:2. Paul speaks to them as fellow Jews, as Stephen did.

decisions.choice: have lived as a citizen: have conducted my life as a member of God's people, keeping my duties
decisions.reason: The verb means to live as a citizen of a community and to conduct oneself accordingly (Philippians 1:27). Paul claims he has lived faithfully as a Jew before God, the charge of 21:28 being that he had not.

decisions.choice: in all good conscience: with nothing on my conscience
decisions.reason: Paul says his conscience does not accuse him, as in 24:16. He does not claim to have been without sin (compare 22:4, 26:9-11).

decisions.choice: all my life I have done what I knew God wanted me to do
alternatives: I have lived as a citizen before God
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what living as a citizen before God means here, as the meaning note explains.

records.heading: Paul before the council

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἀρχιερεὺς Ἁνανίας ἐπέταξεν τοῖς παρεστῶσιν αὐτῷ τύπτειν αὐτοῦ τὸ στόμα.
records.gloss: The then high priest Ananias commanded those standing by him to strike of him the mouth.
pieces: At that, Ananias the high priest told the men standing near Paul to hit him in the mouth.

L.2: And the high priest Ananias commanded those standing by him to strike his mouth.

R.2: Then Ananias the high priest told the men standing beside Paul to hit him on the mouth.

decisions.choice: Ananias: the high priest of the time, son of Nedebaeus
decisions.reason: Josephus names Ananias son of Nedebaeus as high priest from about AD 47 (Antiquities 20.103). He is not the Annas of 4:6 or Luke 3:2. Josephus also says he was killed by rebels at the start of the war with Rome (Jewish War 2.441).

decisions.choice: those standing by him: the men standing near Paul
decisions.reason: The pronoun most naturally points to Paul, who has just spoken; the order is to strike Paul's mouth. Either way the men were attendants of the council.

decisions.choice: strike his mouth: a blow to silence and rebuke a speaker
decisions.reason: A slap on the mouth punished speech held to be insolent, as when an officer struck Jesus before the high priest (John 18:22).

decisions.choice: near Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Paul, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: τότε ὁ Παῦλος πρὸς αὐτὸν εἶπεν· Τύπτειν σε μέλλει ὁ θεός, τοῖχε κεκονιαμένε· καὶ σὺ κάθῃ κρίνων με κατὰ τὸν νόμον, καὶ παρανομῶν κελεύεις με τύπτεσθαι;
records.gloss: Then Paul to him said, To strike you is about God, wall whitewashed; and you sit judging me according to the law, and violating law command me to be struck?
pieces: Then Paul said to him, "God will strike you in turn, you whitewashed wall! You are seated to try me by the law, and you break that same law by having me hit?"

L.3: Then Paul said to him, "God is going to strike you, [you] whitewashed wall! And do you sit judging me according to the law, and, breaking the law, order me to be struck?"

R.3: Then Paul said to him, "God will strike you! You are like a dirty wall that has been painted white to hide the dirt. You sit there to judge me by God's law. But you broke that law when you told them to hit me!"

decisions.choice: God is going to strike you: a warning of God's judgment
decisions.reason: The verb of striking is the same one the high priest used. Paul answers blow for blow: God will strike the one who ordered him struck. The words read as a prediction of judgment, though they may also be heard as an angry curse, which would suit Paul's apology in 23:5.

decisions.choice: whitewashed wall: a fair outside covering what is unsound
alternatives: a plain insult with no background
decisions.reason: Ezekiel 13:10-15 speaks of a flimsy wall daubed with whitewash that God will tear down, a picture of false prophets. Jesus called the Pharisees whitewashed tombs (Matthew 23:27). Paul accuses the high priest of the same pretense.

decisions.choice: judging by the law and breaking the law: striking an accused man before he was convicted
alternatives: breaking a rule of procedure only
decisions.reason: The law required judges to judge fairly (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:16-17) and allowed a beating only after a verdict (Deuteronomy 25:1-2). Paul had not yet been heard.

decisions.choice: God will strike you in turn
alternatives: God is going to strike you
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "in turn" to show that Paul uses the same verb the high priest used, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: You are like a dirty wall that has been painted white to hide the dirt
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture, as the meaning note does.

records.source: οἱ δὲ παρεστῶτες εἶπαν· Τὸν ἀρχιερέα τοῦ θεοῦ λοιδορεῖς;
records.gloss: Those then standing by said, The high priest of God do you insult?
pieces: Those standing by said, "You insult God's own high priest?"

L.4: And those standing by said, "Do you insult the high priest of God?"

R.4: The men standing near Paul said, "Why are you insulting God's high priest?"

decisions.choice: insult: speak abusively to someone
decisions.reason: The verb means to revile or abuse someone to his face. The bystanders treat Paul's words as an offense against God, whose high priest Ananias was.

decisions.choice: a question of outrage: how can you speak so?
decisions.reason: The question is a rebuke, not a real inquiry.

records.source: ἔφη τε ὁ Παῦλος· Οὐκ ᾔδειν, ἀδελφοί, ὅτι ἐστὶν ἀρχιερεύς· γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι Ἄρχοντα τοῦ λαοῦ σου οὐκ ἐρεῖς κακῶς.
records.gloss: Said then Paul, Not I knew, brothers, that he is high priest; it has been written for that, [The] ruler of the people of you not you shall speak of evilly.
pieces: Paul answered, "Brothers, I was not aware that he was the high priest. For Scripture says, 'Never speak ill of one who rules your people.'"

L.5: And Paul said, "I did not know, brothers, that he is [the] high priest, for it is written, 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.'"

R.5: Paul said, "Brothers, I did not know that he was the high priest. The Scriptures say, 'Do not speak badly of anyone who leads your people.'"

decisions.choice: I did not know that he is high priest: Paul did not recognize him as the high priest
alternatives: irony: such a man cannot be high priest
decisions.reason: The words are plain: Paul says he did not know. He may not have known Ananias by sight, or not known who gave the order in a crowded meeting the tribune had called. Some read the words as irony, that a man who acts so cannot be high priest. The text does not say, and the apology that follows reads as sincere.

decisions.choice: a quotation of Exodus 22:28
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the Greek of Exodus 22:28 (22:27 in the Hebrew numbering), which forbids cursing God or a ruler of the people. By quoting the law he shows he keeps it, even toward a judge who has broken it.

decisions.choice: brothers: the members of the council, all men
decisions.reason: As in 23:1, Paul addresses the men of the council as fellow Jews.

decisions.choice: Scripture says
decisions.reason: The formula introduces a quotation from Scripture; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: Γνοὺς δὲ ὁ Παῦλος ὅτι τὸ ἓν μέρος ἐστὶν Σαδδουκαίων τὸ δὲ ἕτερον Φαρισαίων ἔκραζεν ἐν τῷ συνεδρίῳ· Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί, ἐγὼ Φαρισαῖός εἰμι, υἱὸς Φαρισαίων· περὶ ἐλπίδος καὶ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν ἐγὼ κρίνομαι.
records.gloss: Having known then Paul that the one part is of Sadducees, the but other of Pharisees, he was crying out in the council, Men, brothers, I a Pharisee am, son of Pharisees; concerning hope and resurrection of [the] dead I am being judged.
pieces: Aware that the council was made up partly of Sadducees and partly of Pharisees, Paul called out to them, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, born to a family of Pharisees. It is over the hope of the dead rising that I am on trial."

L.6: And Paul, knowing that one part was of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, began crying out in the council, "Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; concerning [the] hope and resurrection of [the] dead I am being judged."

R.6: Paul knew that some of the council members were Sadducees and some were Pharisees. So he shouted to them, "My brothers, I am a Pharisee, and my family were Pharisees. I am on trial because I hope that dead people will rise to life again."

decisions.choice: Sadducees and Pharisees: the two main parties in the council
decisions.reason: The Sadducees were the party of the leading priestly families (5:17); the Pharisees were teachers devoted to the law and its traditions, and many scribes belonged to them (23:9). Both sat in the council (5:34).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "a son of Pharisees"
alternatives: many manuscripts read "a son of a Pharisee"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have the singular, "the son of a Pharisee". Others, some of them early, have the plural, meaning that Paul came from a family of Pharisees. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: hope and resurrection: the hope that the dead will be raised
decisions.reason: The two nouns most likely express one idea, the hope of resurrection, as in 24:15 and 26:6-8. Paul's hope rests on Jesus, whom he had seen risen (22:6-10).

decisions.choice: Men, brothers: the council, all men
alternatives: an address to a mixed audience
decisions.reason: As in 23:1, the hearers are the members of the council.

decisions.choice: It is over the hope of the dead rising that I am on trial
alternatives: I am being judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the Greek stress on the subject of the trial, which stands first.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος ἐγένετο στάσις τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ Σαδδουκαίων, καὶ ἐσχίσθη τὸ πλῆθος.
records.gloss: This then of him saying arose a dissension of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and was divided the assembly.
pieces: As soon as he said this, the Pharisees and Sadducees began to quarrel, and the gathering split in two.

L.7: And when he said this, a dispute arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.

R.7: When he said that, the Pharisees and the Sadducees started to argue with each other. The council split into two groups.

decisions.choice: dispute: a violent quarrel
decisions.reason: The word is used of riots and fierce strife (15:2, 19:40). In 23:10 the dispute grows so violent that the tribune fears for Paul's life.

decisions.choice: assembly: the gathered council
decisions.reason: The word means a large gathering. Here it is the council meeting, whose members split along party lines.

records.source: Σαδδουκαῖοι μὲν γὰρ λέγουσιν μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν μήτε ἄγγελον μήτε πνεῦμα, Φαρισαῖοι δὲ ὁμολογοῦσιν τὰ ἀμφότερα.
records.gloss: Sadducees for say not there to be resurrection nor angel nor spirit, Pharisees but confess both.
pieces: The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, and neither angel nor spirit, but the Pharisees hold to both, the resurrection and the world of spirits.

L.8: For Sadducees say [that there is] no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but Pharisees acknowledge both.

R.8: The Sadducees say that dead people do not rise again. They also say that there are no angels or spirits. But the Pharisees believe in all of these.

decisions.choice: the Sadducees denied resurrection, and the existence of angels and spirits
decisions.reason: Luke says the Sadducees deny the resurrection (Luke 20:27). Josephus says they held that the soul perishes with the body (Antiquities 18.16). What they denied about angels and spirits is not known from other sources; it may be that they rejected any life of the dead as angel or spirit.

decisions.choice: both: the resurrection on the one hand, and angels and spirits on the other
decisions.reason: The word means both of two. Angel and spirit are taken together as one category, set beside the resurrection. In effect the Pharisees affirm all three.

decisions.choice: acknowledge: confess as true, hold as a belief
decisions.reason: The verb means to declare openly what one holds.

decisions.choice: both, the resurrection and the world of spirits
decisions.reason: Balanced names the two things meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: ἐγένετο δὲ κραυγὴ μεγάλη, καὶ ἀναστάντες τινὲς τῶν γραμματέων τοῦ μέρους τῶν Φαρισαίων διεμάχοντο λέγοντες· Οὐδὲν κακὸν εὑρίσκομεν ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τούτῳ· εἰ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ ἢ ἄγγελος πολλῆς δὲ γινομένης στάσεως φοβηθεὶς ὁ χιλίαρχος μὴ διασπασθῇ ὁ Παῦλος ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἐκέλευσεν τὸ στράτευμα καταβὰν ἁρπάσαι αὐτὸν ἐκ μέσου αὐτῶν, ἄγειν τε εἰς τὴν παρεμβολήν.
records.gloss: Arose then a clamor great, and having risen some of the scribes of the party of the Pharisees were contending, saying, Nothing evil we find in the man this; if then a spirit spoke to him or an angel? \v 10 Great then arising dissension, having feared the tribune lest should be torn apart Paul by them, commanded the troop having gone down to seize him from midst of them, to bring then into the barracks.
pieces: The shouting grew loud, and some experts in the law from the Pharisees' party got to their feet and fought the point: "We see no fault in this man. And if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, what then?"
The dispute became so fierce that the tribune feared Paul would be pulled apart between them. He told the troops to go down, seize Paul out of the middle of them, and take him into the barracks.

L.9: And a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the party of the Pharisees stood up and were contending fiercely, saying, "We find nothing evil in this man. And what if a spirit spoke to him, or an angel?"
L.10: And when the dispute became great, the tribune, fearing that Paul would be torn apart by them, commanded the troop to go down and take him by force from their midst and bring [him] into the barracks.

R.9: There was a lot of shouting. Some teachers of the law who were Pharisees stood up and argued strongly. They said, "We do not find anything wrong with this man. Maybe a spirit or an angel really did speak to him!"
R.10: The argument got so bad that the tribune was afraid they would tear Paul apart. So he ordered his soldiers to go down and pull Paul away from them. They took him into the barracks.

decisions.choice: what if a spirit or an angel spoke to him: the sentence is left unfinished
decisions.reason: The Pharisees break off, leaving the conclusion unsaid: then we should be careful how we treat him. They may be thinking of Paul's account of the voice on the road to Damascus (22:6-10).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: the sentence ends with "or an angel"
alternatives: many manuscripts add "let us not fight against God"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, complete the sentence with "let us not fight against God", which recalls Gamaliel's words in 5:39. Earlier manuscripts lack it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the tribune: the Roman officer commanding the garrison in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The title means commander of a thousand. He commanded the cohort in the Antonia fortress beside the temple (21:31-32). His name, Claudius Lysias, is given in 23:26.

decisions.choice: the barracks: the soldiers' quarters in the Antonia fortress
decisions.reason: The fortress overlooked the temple courts, and steps led down from it (21:34-40).

decisions.choice: take him by force: snatch him away
decisions.reason: The verb means to seize quickly and forcibly; the soldiers rescue Paul rather than arrest him.

decisions.choice: experts in the law (B); teachers of the law (R)
decisions.reason: As at 4:5, Balanced and Readable say what scribes were.

decisions.choice: Maybe a spirit or an angel really did speak to him!
alternatives: what if a spirit spoke to him, or an angel?
decisions.reason: Readable turns the unfinished question into a plain statement of what the Pharisees allow, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: Τῇ δὲ ἐπιούσῃ νυκτὶ ἐπιστὰς αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος εἶπεν· Θάρσει, ὡς γὰρ διεμαρτύρω τὰ περὶ ἐμοῦ εἰς Ἰερουσαλὴμ οὕτω σε δεῖ καὶ εἰς Ῥώμην μαρτυρῆσαι.
records.gloss: The then following night having stood by him the Lord said, Take courage, as for you fully testified the things about me in Jerusalem, so you it is necessary also in Rome to testify.
pieces: The following night the Lord came and stood beside Paul. "Take courage," {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said. "Just as you have borne witness to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in Jerusalem, you must bear witness in Rome as well."

L.11: And on the following night the Lord stood by him and said, "Take courage, for as you have fully testified to the things about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome."

R.11: The next night the Lord Jesus came and stood beside Paul. He said, "Be brave! You have told people about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} here in Jerusalem. You must tell people about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in Rome too."

decisions.choice: the Lord: the risen Jesus
decisions.reason: The Lord speaks of the witness Paul has given "about me", that is, about Jesus (22:18-21). He appeared to Paul in a vision before, at Corinth (18:9-10).

decisions.choice: take courage: do not lose heart
decisions.reason: The word is a call to be brave, as Jesus said it to those he healed and to his frightened disciples (Matthew 9:2; Mark 6:50).

decisions.choice: you must also testify in Rome: it is God's plan that Paul bear witness in Rome
decisions.reason: The word for "must" often expresses God's will in Luke's writings (1:16, 3:21). Paul had planned to see Rome (19:21); now the Lord confirms it, and the rest of Acts leads there (28:14-16).

decisions.choice: the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, as the meaning note explains.

records.heading: Take courage

records.source: Γενομένης δὲ ἡμέρας ποιήσαντες συστροφὴν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἀνεθεμάτισαν ἑαυτοὺς λέγοντες μήτε φαγεῖν μήτε πιεῖν ἕως οὗ ἀποκτείνωσιν τὸν Παῦλον.
records.gloss: When it was then day having made a conspiracy the Jews put under a curse themselves, saying neither to eat nor to drink until that they should kill Paul.
pieces: When day came, a group of Jews banded together and swore an oath, calling down a curse on themselves if they ate or drank anything before they had killed Paul.

L.12: And when it was day, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves under a curse, saying [that they would] neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

R.12: The next morning some Jewish men made a secret plan to kill Paul. They made a solemn promise and asked God to curse them if they ate or drank anything before they had killed Paul.

decisions.choice: bound themselves under a curse: swore an oath, calling God's curse on themselves if they broke it
decisions.reason: The verb comes from the word for a thing devoted to destruction (anathema). Those who swore so asked God to destroy them if they did not do what they vowed. Their oath was not kept, but the text does not say what became of them.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the particular Jews who made the plot
decisions.reason: Luke means the opponents of Paul in Jerusalem, more than forty men (23:13), not the Jewish people as a whole.

decisions.choice: conspiracy: a secret plot
decisions.reason: The word means a gathering of people, here banded together in secret.

decisions.choice: a group of Jews (B); some Jewish men (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that only some Jews are meant, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: made a secret plan to kill Paul
decisions.reason: Readable says what the plot was for, which the sentence goes on to state.

records.heading: More than forty men under a curse

records.source: ἦσαν δὲ πλείους τεσσεράκοντα οἱ ταύτην τὴν συνωμοσίαν ποιησάμενοι·
records.gloss: There were then more than forty those this plot having made.
pieces: More than forty men took part in this plot.

L.13: And there were more than forty who made this plot.

R.13: More than forty men joined in this plan.

decisions.choice: more than forty: the number of the plotters
decisions.reason: The young man repeats the number to the tribune (23:21), where they are called men.

decisions.choice: men
decisions.reason: The plotters are called men in 23:21.

records.source: οἵτινες προσελθόντες τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσιν καὶ τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις εἶπαν· Ἀναθέματι ἀνεθεματίσαμεν ἑαυτοὺς μηδενὸς γεύσασθαι ἕως οὗ ἀποκτείνωμεν τὸν Παῦλον.
records.gloss: Who having come to the chief priests and the elders said, With a curse we have put under a curse ourselves nothing to taste until that we should kill Paul.
pieces: They went to the chief priests and the elders and told them, "We have put ourselves under a solemn curse: we will not taste a thing until we have killed Paul.

L.14: They came to the chief priests and the elders and said, "With a curse we have put ourselves under a curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

R.14: They went to the leading priests and the elders and said, "We have made a very serious promise to God. We will not eat anything until we have killed Paul.

decisions.choice: with a curse we have cursed ourselves: we have sworn a most solemn oath
decisions.reason: Repeating the verb with its own noun makes it emphatic, as in 5:28.

decisions.choice: the chief priests and the elders: the leaders of the council
decisions.reason: The plotters go to the council's leaders, whom they expect to help them. The Pharisee scribes who had defended Paul (23:9) are not named.

decisions.choice: leading priests
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plain word for the priests of the leading families.

decisions.choice: We have made a very serious promise to God
alternatives: With a curse we have put ourselves under a curse
decisions.reason: Readable says what the oath was, as at 23:12.

records.source: νῦν οὖν ὑμεῖς ἐμφανίσατε τῷ χιλιάρχῳ σὺν τῷ συνεδρίῳ ὅπως καταγάγῃ αὐτὸν εἰς ὑμᾶς ὡς μέλλοντας διαγινώσκειν ἀκριβέστερον τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ· ἡμεῖς δὲ πρὸ τοῦ ἐγγίσαι αὐτὸν ἕτοιμοί ἐσμεν τοῦ ἀνελεῖν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Now therefore you notify the tribune with the council, so that he might bring down him to you as being about to examine more accurately the things about him; we then before the to come near him ready are to kill him.
pieces: So now you and the council must tell the tribune to bring Paul down to you, claiming that you want to look into his case more closely. We will be waiting to kill him before he ever reaches you."

L.15: Now therefore, you, together with the council, notify the tribune so that he may bring him down to you, as though you were going to examine the things about him more accurately; and we, before he comes near, are ready to kill him."

R.15: So you and the council should send a message to the tribune. Ask him to bring Paul down to you. Pretend that you want to ask Paul more questions about his case. We will be ready to kill him on the way, before he gets to you."

decisions.choice: as though you were going to examine: a pretext
decisions.reason: The word "as" marks it as a pretense: the hearing would be a trap.

decisions.choice: bring him down: from the Antonia fortress to the council's meeting place
decisions.reason: The fortress stood above the temple courts, so Paul would be led down (22:30). The plotters meant to attack him on the way.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the person meant.

decisions.choice: on the way
decisions.reason: Readable says where the attack was to happen, which the sentence implies.

records.source: Ἀκούσας δὲ ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀδελφῆς Παύλου τὴν ἐνέδραν παραγενόμενος καὶ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὴν παρεμβολὴν ἀπήγγειλεν τῷ Παύλῳ.
records.gloss: Having heard however the son of the sister of Paul of the ambush, having come and having entered into the barracks reported [it] to Paul.
pieces: But Paul's nephew, the son of his sister, got word of the ambush. He made his way into the barracks and warned Paul.

L.16: But the son of Paul's sister heard of the ambush, and having come and entered into the barracks, he reported [it] to Paul.

R.16: But the son of Paul's sister heard about the plan to attack Paul. So he went to the barracks and told Paul about it.

decisions.choice: the son of Paul's sister: Paul's nephew
decisions.reason: This is the only mention of Paul's family in Jerusalem. Paul had studied there (22:3), and his sister may have lived in the city. How the young man heard of the plot is not said.

decisions.choice: having come: he went to the barracks
alternatives: having been present when the plot was made
decisions.reason: The participle may go with what follows, "he came and went in", or with what goes before, "he heard of it, being present". The first is the more natural reading.

decisions.choice: entered into the barracks: he was allowed to visit Paul
decisions.reason: A Roman citizen held without trial could receive visitors, as Paul later did (24:23).

records.source: προσκαλεσάμενος δὲ ὁ Παῦλος ἕνα τῶν ἑκατονταρχῶν ἔφη· Τὸν νεανίαν τοῦτον ἄπαγε πρὸς τὸν χιλίαρχον, ἔχει γὰρ ἀπαγγεῖλαί τι αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: Having called to [him] then Paul one of the centurions was saying, The young man this take to the tribune, he has for to report something to him.
pieces: Paul called over one of the centurions and said, "Bring this young man to the tribune; he has news for him."

L.17: And Paul, having called one of the centurions, said, "Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him."

R.17: Paul called one of the centurions and said, "Take this young man to the tribune. He has something to tell him."

decisions.choice: centurion: a Roman officer over about a hundred soldiers
decisions.reason: The centurions served under the tribune (21:32, 22:25-26).

decisions.choice: young man: a youth, of unknown age
decisions.reason: The word is used of men up to about thirty; the tribune takes him by the hand (23:19), which may suggest he was young.

records.source: ὁ μὲν οὖν παραλαβὼν αὐτὸν ἤγαγεν πρὸς τὸν χιλίαρχον καὶ φησίν· Ὁ δέσμιος Παῦλος προσκαλεσάμενός με ἠρώτησεν τοῦτον τὸν νεανίαν ἀγαγεῖν πρὸς σέ, ἔχοντά τι λαλῆσαί σοι.
records.gloss: The [one] indeed therefore having taken him brought [him] to the tribune and says, The prisoner Paul having called to me asked this the young man to bring to you, having something to say to you.
pieces: The centurion brought him to the tribune and reported, "The prisoner Paul called me over and asked me to take this young man to you, since he has a message for you."

L.18: So he took him and brought [him] to the tribune and said, "The prisoner Paul called me and asked [me] to bring this young man to you, who has something to say to you."

R.18: So the centurion took the young man to the tribune. He said, "Paul, the prisoner, called me. He asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you."

decisions.choice: prisoner: a man in bonds
decisions.reason: The word means one who is bound. Paul later calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1).

decisions.choice: says: the present tense makes the scene vivid
decisions.reason: Luke switches to the present tense in the middle of the narrative; the sense is past.

decisions.choice: said
decisions.reason: Literal uses the past tense, since English cannot shift tense in this way, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: the centurion
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

records.source: ἐπιλαβόμενος δὲ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ ὁ χιλίαρχος καὶ ἀναχωρήσας κατ’ ἰδίαν ἐπυνθάνετο· Τί ἐστιν ὃ ἔχεις ἀπαγγεῖλαί μοι;
records.gloss: Having taken hold then of the hand of him the tribune, and having withdrawn in private, was inquiring, What is it that you have to report to me?
pieces: The tribune took hold of his hand, led him off to one side by themselves, and asked him, "What is this news you have for me?"

L.19: And the tribune took him by the hand and, having withdrawn privately, began to inquire, "What is it that you have to report to me?"

R.19: The tribune took the young man by the hand and led him to a place where they could be alone. He asked, "What do you want to tell me?"

decisions.choice: took him by the hand: a kind and reassuring gesture
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to take hold of firmly, but here the tribune draws the young man aside in a friendly way, perhaps to put him at ease.

decisions.choice: withdrew privately: went aside where no one could hear
decisions.reason: The phrase means in private, as in Luke 9:10.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ὅτι Οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι συνέθεντο τοῦ ἐρωτῆσαί σε ὅπως αὔριον τὸν Παῦλον καταγάγῃς εἰς τὸ συνέδριον ὡς μέλλον τι ἀκριβέστερον πυνθάνεσθαι περὶ αὐτοῦ·
records.gloss: He said then that, The Jews agreed to ask you that tomorrow Paul you might bring down to the council as being about something more accurately to inquire about him.
pieces: He answered, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as if the council meant to look more carefully into his case.

L.20: And he said, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it were going to inquire somewhat more accurately about him.

R.20: He said, "Some Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul to the council tomorrow. They will pretend that the council wants to ask him more questions.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "as though it were going to", that is, the council
alternatives: other manuscripts read "as though you were going to", or "as though they were going to"
decisions.reason: The participle differs among manuscripts. The SBLGNT form agrees with "the council"; others make the tribune or the Jews the subject. The pretext is the same either way. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the plotters and the leaders they had won over
decisions.reason: As in 23:12, Luke means the particular Jews involved.

decisions.choice: Some Jews
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that only some Jews are meant, as at 23:12.

records.source: σὺ οὖν μὴ πεισθῇς αὐτοῖς, ἐνεδρεύουσιν γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐξ αὐτῶν ἄνδρες πλείους τεσσεράκοντα, οἵτινες ἀνεθεμάτισαν ἑαυτοὺς μήτε φαγεῖν μήτε πιεῖν ἕως οὗ ἀνέλωσιν αὐτόν, καὶ νῦν εἰσιν ἕτοιμοι προσδεχόμενοι τὴν ἀπὸ σοῦ ἐπαγγελίαν.
records.gloss: You therefore not be persuaded by them; lie in wait for for him of them men more than forty, who put under a curse themselves neither to eat nor to drink until that they have killed him, and now they are ready, awaiting the from you promise.
pieces: Do not let them persuade you. More than forty of their men are lying in wait for him. They have sworn under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed him, and they are ready now, only waiting for you to say yes."

L.21: So do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty men of them are lying in wait for him, who have put themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him; and now they are ready, waiting for the promise from you."

R.21: But do not do what they ask! More than forty of them are hiding and waiting to attack Paul. They have made a promise not to eat or drink anything until they have killed him. They are ready right now. They are only waiting for you to agree."

decisions.choice: the promise from you: your consent to the request
alternatives: a promise the tribune had already made
decisions.reason: The tribune has promised nothing yet; the plotters wait for him to grant the council's request.

decisions.choice: lie in wait: are waiting in ambush
decisions.reason: The verb is related to the noun "ambush" in 23:16.

decisions.choice: for you to say yes (B); for you to agree (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the promise was, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: ὁ μὲν οὖν χιλίαρχος ἀπέλυσε τὸν νεανίσκον παραγγείλας μηδενὶ ἐκλαλῆσαι ὅτι ταῦτα ἐνεφάνισας πρὸς ἐμέ.
records.gloss: The indeed therefore tribune dismissed the young man, having instructed [him], No one to tell that these things you reported to me.
pieces: The tribune sent the young man away with a warning: "Do not let anyone know you told me about this."

L.22: So the tribune dismissed the young man, having ordered [him], "Tell no one that you have reported these things to me."

R.22: The tribune let the young man go. He told him, "Do not tell anyone that you told me about this."

decisions.choice: the order begins as reported speech and ends as direct speech
decisions.reason: "To tell no one" is reported, but "you have reported to me" is in the tribune's own words. Luke slips from one to the other, as in 1:4 and 14:22; the sense is a direct command.

records.source: Καὶ προσκαλεσάμενός τινας δύο τῶν ἑκατονταρχῶν εἶπεν· Ἑτοιμάσατε στρατιώτας διακοσίους ὅπως πορευθῶσιν ἕως Καισαρείας, καὶ ἱππεῖς ἑβδομήκοντα καὶ δεξιολάβους διακοσίους, ἀπὸ τρίτης ὥρας τῆς νυκτός, κτήνη τε παραστῆσαι ἵνα ἐπιβιβάσαντες τὸν Παῦλον διασώσωσι πρὸς Φήλικα τὸν ἡγεμόνα, γράψας ἐπιστολὴν ἔχουσαν τὸν τύπον τοῦτον·
records.gloss: And having called to [him] certain two of the centurions he said, Prepare soldiers two hundred so that they might go as far as Caesarea, and horsemen seventy and spearmen two hundred, from third hour of the night, \v 24 mounts then to provide, so that having set on Paul they might bring [him] safely to Felix the governor, \v 25 having written a letter having the form this:
pieces: Then he summoned two of his centurions and told them, "Have 200 soldiers ready to leave for Caesarea at nine o'clock tonight, with seventy horsemen and 200 spearmen."
He also had them provide mounts for Paul to ride, so that he would reach Felix the governor safely.
And he wrote a letter that went like this:

L.23: And having called two of the centurions, he said, "Get ready 200 soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, and seventy horsemen and 200 spearmen, from the third hour of the night."
L.24: And [he told them] to provide mounts, so that they might set Paul on [one] and bring [him] safely to Felix the governor,
L.25: having written a letter having this form:

R.23: Then the tribune called two of his centurions. He said, "Get 200 soldiers ready to go to Caesarea. Take seventy soldiers on horses and 200 soldiers with spears too. Be ready to leave at nine o'clock tonight."
R.24: He told them to get horses for Paul to ride. They were to take him safely to Felix, the governor.
R.25: The tribune wrote a letter to Felix. This is what it said:

decisions.choice: spearmen: a kind of lightly armed soldier, perhaps carrying spears
decisions.reason: The word is very rare and its meaning is not known for certain. It may mean those who hold something in the right hand, such as a spear. Some think of soldiers leading spare horses. The text tells only that they were part of the escort.

decisions.choice: the third hour of the night: about nine o'clock in the evening
decisions.reason: The night was counted from sunset, about six o'clock. The escort left under cover of darkness, out of the plotters' sight.

decisions.choice: a strong escort: 470 men in all
decisions.reason: The tribune took the plot seriously. Some of the escort went only part of the way and returned the next day (23:32).

decisions.choice: Felix the governor: the Roman governor of Judea, who lived at Caesarea
decisions.reason: Antonius Felix governed Judea in the fifties AD. The Roman historian Tacitus describes him as a former slave who ruled harshly (Histories 5.9). Caesarea, on the coast, was the seat of the Roman governors (12:19).

decisions.choice: provide mounts: the tribune's order continues in reported speech
decisions.reason: The infinitive depends on "he said": the tribune told them to provide mounts.

decisions.choice: mounts: animals for riding
decisions.reason: The word means beasts used for riding or carrying, such as horses or mules. The plural may mean more than one, for Paul and his things, or for changes on the way.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: no further explanation
alternatives: one manuscript adds why the tribune acted: he feared that the Jews would seize and kill Paul and that he would then be accused of taking bribes
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and some other witnesses add this reason at 23:24. Most manuscripts lack it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: having this form: to this effect
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean a letter in these words or a letter with this content. Luke may give the substance of it.

decisions.choice: at nine o'clock tonight
alternatives: from the third hour of the night
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern time, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: soldiers on horses; soldiers with spears
decisions.reason: Readable describes each kind of soldier.

decisions.choice: horses
decisions.reason: Readable uses the commonest riding animal; the word could also mean mules.

decisions.choice: [he told them]
decisions.reason: Literal shows in brackets that the reported command depends on "he said".

records.heading: Sent by night to Felix the governor

records.source: Κλαύδιος Λυσίας τῷ κρατίστῳ ἡγεμόνι Φήλικι χαίρειν.
records.gloss: Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix, greetings.
pieces: "Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix: greetings.

L.26: "Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent governor Felix: greetings.

R.26: "From Claudius Lysias, to Felix, the honored governor. Greetings!

decisions.choice: the usual opening of a Greek letter: sender, recipient, greeting
decisions.reason: Letters began this way, as the letter of the Jerusalem church does (15:23) and James 1:1.

decisions.choice: Claudius Lysias: the tribune's name
decisions.reason: Lysias is a Greek name. The tribune had bought his Roman citizenship (22:28), and new citizens often took the family name of the emperor, here Claudius, who reigned AD 41-54.

decisions.choice: most excellent: a title of respect for high Roman officials
decisions.reason: The same title is given to Felix (24:3), to Festus (26:25) and to Theophilus (Luke 1:3).

decisions.choice: honored
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plain word of respect.

records.source: τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον συλλημφθέντα ὑπὸ τῶν Ἰουδαίων καὶ μέλλοντα ἀναιρεῖσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἐπιστὰς σὺν τῷ στρατεύματι ἐξειλάμην, μαθὼν ὅτι Ῥωμαῖός ἐστιν, βουλόμενός τε ἐπιγνῶναι τὴν αἰτίαν δι’ ἣν ἐνεκάλουν αὐτῷ, κατήγαγον εἰς τὸ συνέδριον αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: The man this having been seized by the Jews and being about to be killed by them, having come up with the troop I rescued, having learned that a Roman he is; \v 28 wishing then to know the charge on account of which they were accusing him, I brought [him] down to the council of them;
pieces: The Jews had taken hold of this man and were on the verge of killing him. I came on the scene with the troops and pulled him out of their hands, having found out that he was a Roman citizen.
Since I wanted to learn the grounds of their charges against him, I had him brought before their council.

L.27: This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them, when I came up with the troop and rescued [him], having learned that he is a Roman.
L.28: And wishing to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought [him] down to their council.

R.27: The Jews grabbed this man and were going to kill him. But I came with my soldiers and saved him. I had found out that he is a Roman citizen.
R.28: I wanted to know what they said he had done wrong. So I took him to their council.

decisions.choice: having learned that he is a Roman: the letter puts this before the rescue
alternatives: the tribune learned it later and the letter says so
decisions.reason: In Luke's account the tribune learned that Paul was a citizen only after he had ordered him flogged (22:25-29). The letter leaves out the flogging and makes the rescue seem the act of an officer protecting a citizen. The participle may be read loosely as "since I learned", but the order of events is still favorable to the writer.

decisions.choice: a Roman: a Roman citizen
decisions.reason: The word means a citizen of Rome, as in 16:37 and 22:25-29.

decisions.choice: the events of 21:30-36
decisions.reason: The crowd seized Paul in the temple and were trying to kill him when the tribune came with soldiers (21:30-32).

decisions.choice: I brought him down to their council: the hearing of 22:30-23:10
decisions.reason: The tribune had called the council to learn what Paul was accused of (22:30).

decisions.choice: Roman citizen
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what being a Roman meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: ὃν εὗρον ἐγκαλούμενον περὶ ζητημάτων τοῦ νόμου αὐτῶν, μηδὲν δὲ ἄξιον θανάτου ἢ δεσμῶν ἔχοντα ἔγκλημα.
records.gloss: whom I found being accused concerning questions of the law of them, no however worthy of death or of chains having accusation.
pieces: I found he was being accused over points of their own law, but with nothing that called for death or chains.

L.29: I found him to be accused about questions of their law, but having no charge [against him] worthy of death or chains.

R.29: I learned that they were accusing him about questions of their own Jewish law. But he had done nothing that deserved death or prison.

decisions.choice: whom: the letter's sentence continues from 23:28
decisions.reason: The relative pronoun links this to the council hearing of 23:28; the SBLGNT ends the sentence at 23:28 and starts a new one here.

decisions.choice: no charge worthy of death or chains: Paul had done nothing that Roman law punishes
alternatives: Paul was innocent before Jewish law
decisions.reason: Roman officials declare Paul innocent again and again (25:25, 26:31-32), as Pilate did Jesus (Luke 23:4, 23:14-15, 23:22).

decisions.choice: questions of their law: disputes about the Jewish law and beliefs
decisions.reason: Gallio said the same of such charges at Corinth (18:14-15).

decisions.choice: their own Jewish law
decisions.reason: Readable names the law meant.

decisions.choice: prison
decisions.reason: Readable says what chains stand for here.

records.source: μηνυθείσης δέ μοι ἐπιβουλῆς εἰς τὸν ἄνδρα ἔσεσθαι ἐξαυτῆς ἔπεμψα πρὸς σέ, παραγγείλας καὶ τοῖς κατηγόροις λέγειν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐπὶ σοῦ.
records.gloss: It having been disclosed then to me of a plot against the man would be, at once I sent [him] to you, having instructed also the accusers to speak the things against him before you.
pieces: Word reached me that a plot was being laid against him, so I am sending him to you straight away, and I have told his accusers to state their case against him in your presence."

L.30: And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent [him] to you at once, also instructing his accusers to speak against him before you."

R.30: Then someone told me that there was a plan to kill this man. So I am sending him to you right away. I have also told the people who accuse him to come and tell you what they have against him."

decisions.choice: I sent: the writer speaks from the time the letter is read
decisions.reason: Letters often use the past tense for what is happening as the letter is written, since it will be past when it is read. Paul travels with the letter.

decisions.choice: instructing his accusers: they too are told to go to Felix
decisions.reason: The accusers come five days later (24:1).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: the letter ends without a farewell
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, end the letter with a word meaning "Farewell", as the letter in 15:29 ends. Others, some of them early, lack it. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: I am sending
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the tense English uses in a letter for this, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: a plan to kill this man
decisions.reason: Readable says what the plot was.

records.source: Οἱ μὲν οὖν στρατιῶται κατὰ τὸ διατεταγμένον αὐτοῖς ἀναλαβόντες τὸν Παῦλον ἤγαγον διὰ νυκτὸς εἰς τὴν Ἀντιπατρίδα·
records.gloss: The indeed therefore soldiers according to that having been ordered them, having taken Paul, brought [him] by night to Antipatris.
pieces: The soldiers followed their instructions: they took charge of Paul and marched him through the night to Antipatris.

L.31: So the soldiers, according to what had been ordered them, took Paul and brought [him] by night to Antipatris.

R.31: The soldiers did what they were told. They took Paul and traveled all night to the town of Antipatris.

decisions.choice: Antipatris: a town on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea
decisions.reason: Herod the Great built it and named it after his father Antipater (Josephus, Antiquities 16.142). It lay about two thirds of the way to Caesarea, where the hill country gives way to the plain.

decisions.choice: by night: during the night
alternatives: the whole distance in one night
decisions.reason: Antipatris is a long way from Jerusalem for one night's march. Luke may mean they set out by night and reached Antipatris the next day; the text does not say.

decisions.choice: the town of
decisions.reason: Readable says what Antipatris was.

records.source: τῇ δὲ ἐπαύριον ἐάσαντες τοὺς ἱππεῖς ἀπέρχεσθαι σὺν αὐτῷ ὑπέστρεψαν εἰς τὴν παρεμβολήν·
records.gloss: On the then next day having let the horsemen to go with him they returned to the barracks.
pieces: The next day they left the horsemen to go on with him and went back to the barracks themselves.

L.32: And on the next day, having let the horsemen go on with him, they returned to the barracks.

R.32: The next day the soldiers on foot went back to the barracks in Jerusalem. The soldiers on horses went on with Paul.

decisions.choice: they returned: the soldiers on foot and the spearmen
decisions.reason: Once the dangerous hill country was behind them, the horsemen alone took Paul on to Caesarea.

decisions.choice: the soldiers on foot; in Jerusalem; with Paul
decisions.reason: Readable names who returned and where, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: οἵτινες εἰσελθόντες εἰς τὴν Καισάρειαν καὶ ἀναδόντες τὴν ἐπιστολὴν τῷ ἡγεμόνι παρέστησαν καὶ τὸν Παῦλον αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: who having entered into Caesarea and having delivered the letter to the governor presented also Paul to him.
pieces: When the horsemen reached Caesarea, they handed the letter to the governor and brought Paul before him as well.

L.33: They entered Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor and also presented Paul to him.

R.33: The soldiers on horses arrived in Caesarea. They gave the letter to the governor, and they brought Paul to him too.

decisions.choice: who: the horsemen
decisions.reason: The relative pronoun points back to the horsemen of 23:32.

decisions.choice: Caesarea: the port city that was the seat of the Roman governor
decisions.reason: This is Caesarea on the coast, where Philip lived (21:8), not Caesarea Philippi in the north.

decisions.choice: the horsemen (B); the soldiers on horses (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject.

records.source: ἀναγνοὺς δὲ καὶ ἐπερωτήσας ἐκ ποίας ἐπαρχείας ἐστὶν καὶ πυθόμενος ὅτι ἀπὸ Κιλικίας, Διακούσομαί σου, ἔφη, ὅταν καὶ οἱ κατήγοροί σου παραγένωνται· κελεύσας ἐν τῷ πραιτωρίῳ τοῦ Ἡρῴδου φυλάσσεσθαι αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Having read [it] then and having asked from what province he is, and having learned that from Cilicia, \v 35 I will hear you fully, he was saying, when also the accusers of you may have arrived; having commanded in the praetorium of Herod to be guarded him.
pieces: After reading the letter, the governor asked what province Paul belonged to, and learned that it was Cilicia.
"I will give you a full hearing," he said, "once your accusers are here as well." Then he gave orders for Paul to be held under guard in Herod's praetorium.

L.34: And having read [it] and asked from what province he was, and having learned that [he was] from Cilicia,
L.35: he said, "I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive," having ordered him to be guarded in the praetorium of Herod.

R.34: The governor read the letter. Then he asked Paul what part of the empire he came from. He found out that Paul was from Cilicia.
R.35: So the governor said, "I will listen to your case when the people who accuse you get here." Then he ordered his soldiers to guard Paul in the palace that King Herod had built.

decisions.choice: from what province: a question of who should hear the case
decisions.reason: A Roman governor could hear a case himself or send it to the governor of the accused's home province, as Pilate sent Jesus to Herod when he learned he was a Galilean (Luke 23:6-7). Luke does not say why Felix asked. Cilicia was Paul's home, Tarsus being its city (21:39, 22:3).

decisions.choice: I will hear you fully: I will give your case a proper hearing
decisions.reason: The verb is a legal one, to hear a case through to the end.

decisions.choice: the praetorium of Herod: the palace Herod the Great built at Caesarea, used as the governor's headquarters
decisions.reason: A praetorium was the residence of a Roman governor (compare Mark 15:16). Paul was held there, not in a common jail.

decisions.choice: the governor; the letter
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the reader and what he read.

decisions.choice: the palace that King Herod had built
decisions.reason: Readable says what the praetorium was, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: what part of the empire
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word province.
